units.full: Beta-blockers competitively antagonise beta-adrenergic receptors, decreasing cyclic AMP and intracellular calcium in cardiac myocytes and vascular smooth muscle. Cardioselective beta-1 blockers (metoprolol, bisoprolol, atenolol, esmolol) lower heart rate, contractility, AV nodal conduction, and renin release while largely sparing beta-2 bronchial receptors at standard doses, although selectivity is lost at high doses. Non-selective beta-1 and beta-2 blockers (propranolol, nadolol, timolol) additionally block peripheral beta-2 vasodilation, bronchodilation, and glycogenolysis. Mixed alpha-1 and beta blockers (carvedilol, labetalol) add peripheral vasodilation to reduce afterload. Agents with intrinsic sympathomimetic activity (pindolol, acebutolol) act as partial agonists and produce less resting bradycardia.

units.full: Beta-2 blockade can trigger severe bronchospasm in asthma or reactive COPD, making non-selective beta-blockers contraindicated in asthma. In diabetes, beta-blockers mask adrenergic hypoglycaemia warning signs (tremor, palpitations) while diaphoresis persists because sweating is cholinergic. In cocaine toxicity or untreated phaeochromocytoma, pure beta blockade causes unopposed alpha-1 vasoconstriction and dangerous hypertension. Abrupt withdrawal causes rebound tachycardia and angina due to beta-receptor upregulation: taper over 1 to 2 weeks. Overdose presents with refractory bradycardia, hypotension, and hypoglycaemia; treat with intravenous glucagon (activates adenylyl cyclase independent of beta receptors), atropine, and high-dose insulin euglycaemia.
